name: Locks, Deadlocks and Contention
intent: Know what a lock gives you (one thread at a time), what it costs (waiting, and the chance of waiting forever), and how to choose between one coarse lock and several fine ones.
scenario: Two threads each need two locks, A and B, to move data between two accounts. One version takes them in opposite orders, one in the same order, and one uses a single lock for everything. A second model runs 1 to 16 threads that each do 20 jobs, with 20 ticks of work outside the lock and 2 or 20 ticks inside it.
problem: Locks fix races, and then create two new problems. If two threads each hold one lock and wait for the other's, neither ever moves, and nothing reports an error: the program just stops. And because a lock lets only one thread through at a time, a lock that is busy all the time turns a parallel program back into a queue, so adding threads makes it no faster, or slower.

howItWorks.title: A lock admits one thread at a time
howItWorks.text: A thread that asks for a held lock waits until the holder releases it. That removes races inside the protected section, at the price of making every other thread that needs the same lock wait. The time a thread keeps the lock is the cost to everyone else, so the section should hold only what must be protected.

howItWorks.title: Deadlock needs four things at once
howItWorks.text: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion (the lock admits one), hold-and-wait (a thread keeps what it has while it asks for more), no preemption (locks are not taken away) and a circular wait (A waits for B, B waits for A). Take any one away and it cannot happen. The common fix is to remove the circle.

howItWorks.title: Lock in one global order
howItWorks.text: If every thread takes locks in the same agreed order (say by account id, lowest first), a cycle cannot form, because a thread holding a high lock never waits for a lower one. In the model, opposite order deadlocks in 2 of 6 schedules and the same order in none. A lock taken twice by the same thread deadlocks at once unless the lock is re-entrant.

howItWorks.title: Coarse locks are safe and serial
howItWorks.text: One lock for everything makes deadlock between locks impossible and the code easy to reason about, but every thread queues behind every other, even when they touch different data. Once the lock is busy all the time, throughput is capped at one critical section at a time, whatever the thread count.

howItWorks.title: Fine locks buy parallelism and cost care
howItWorks.text: Several locks, one per piece of data, let threads that touch different data run together. The cost is that an operation needing two locks now needs an order for them, and the code that reads the state may need several locks. Keep critical sections short and never do slow work (a network call, a disk read) while holding a lock, or the lock becomes the bottleneck.

pros: A lock around a critical section makes its read-modify-write safe against any other thread
A fixed lock order removes the circular wait, and so removes deadlock between locks
Fine-grained locks let threads working on different data run at the same time
A single coarse lock is simple and has no lock-order bugs
cons: Threads waiting for a busy lock do no work, so a hot lock caps throughput however many threads you add
A deadlock freezes the threads involved with no error, and may only occur in a few percent of schedules
Fine locks bring lock ordering, and more places to get it wrong
A thread that is slow or paused while holding a lock stalls everyone who needs it
whenToUse: A lock for a critical section that changes several values together, held as briefly as possible
A fixed lock order whenever one operation needs more than one lock
Fine-grained or sharded locks when a profile shows threads waiting on one hot lock
whenNotToUse: A lock around data only one thread touches, or around data that is never changed
Fine-grained locks before you have measured waiting: a coarse lock that is rarely busy costs nothing
A lock held across a slow call to another service: use a copy of the data, or a different design
pitfalls: Taking two locks in different orders in different code paths: it deadlocks only when the timing lines up, so it passes tests
Calling out to unknown code (a callback, a virtual method, an event handler) while holding a lock, which may take another lock
Doing I/O inside a critical section: with 20 ticks inside the lock instead of 2, the model's speedup is stuck at 1.9x from 4 threads up
Taking a non-re-entrant lock you already hold: some locks are re-entrant (C# lock, Java synchronized, Python RLock) and some are not (Python Lock, Go Mutex)
Fixing contention by adding threads: when the lock is the bottleneck, more threads mean a longer queue
Replacing deadlock with a timeout and a retry without backoff: two threads can keep releasing and retaking the same locks without finishing (a livelock)

quiz.question: Two code paths take locks A and B in opposite orders. The service has run for months without a hang, then freezes once. Why did it take so long?
options: The locks wear out after a fixed number of uses, and then stop releasing properly.
Only schedules where each thread gets its first lock before the other gets its second deadlock, and most runs miss that timing.
Deadlock only happens after a runtime has been up for months and its lock table has filled.
A deadlock needs three or more threads, and traffic only reached that level this week.
quiz.explanation: With two threads and opposite orders, the model deadlocks in 2 of 6 schedules: the ones where each thread takes its first lock before the other has taken its second. On a quiet system most runs happen to avoid that timing, so the bug sits in the code until the interleaving appears.

quiz.question: A team replaces 20 fine locks with one global lock to stop deadlocks. Deadlocks stop, but doubling the number of threads no longer increases throughput. Why?
options: A global lock is slower per acquisition than 20 small locks because it is larger in memory.
Threads cannot share a global lock across processor cores, so they all run on one core.
The lock makes each thread run its code twice, once to check and once to commit.
Only one thread can be inside the lock at a time, so the rest queue and the lock is the limit.
quiz.explanation: One lock makes every critical section run one after another. Once the lock is busy all the time, throughput is capped at one critical section at a time, whatever the thread count. Fine locks recover parallelism for threads that touch different data, at the price of needing a lock order.

quiz.question: Which change removes the deadlock between a thread that locks A then B and a thread that locks B then A?
options: Make both threads take the locks in the same fixed order, such as A before B.
Make each thread hold its first lock for a shorter time before asking for the second.
Run the two threads on separate processor cores instead of one.
Give each thread a higher priority, so the scheduler runs it sooner.
quiz.explanation: A fixed order breaks the circular wait, the one condition a deadlock cannot do without. Holding locks for less time only makes the bad timing rarer, and cores or priorities do not change who waits for whom.
